readerAnswers.finding: Women accounted for 26% of U.S. hires into AI occupations in 2025, compared with 50% of hires into other occupations, according to research LinkedIn published on August 18. Its separate international leadership analysis found that women held 13% of top executive AI leadership roles at AI companies. These figures describe who is getting hired and who holds authority.A U.S. Census Bureau report published on August 11 measures something different: how often people use AI at work. Among workers who had used AI for at least one of the tasks surveyed, 30% of men and 17% of women reported using it every day in the previous week. The survey was conducted in March 2026.Those are different groups and different questions. The hiring figures do not cover every job in which someone uses AI. The frequency figures do not measure skill, interest or whether daily use would help someone do her job. Neither report establishes why a particular woman has less access to an opportunity.

readerAnswers.mechanism: Our concern is how employers distribute the opportunities that come with AI: a place on a project, time to learn, a leadership role or a say in how a job changes. Telling women to practise more does not answer who gets those opportunities.Imagine two equally interested colleagues. One is given an approved AI tool, paid time to try it and an invitation to help evaluate a new process. The other is told to keep up, without those arrangements. If the first colleague uses AI more often, that alone would tell us little about the second colleague’s enthusiasm or ability. This is an example of why conditions matter, not a finding about what caused the survey gap.The next decision matters too. If a manager selects a trial team only from people already using the tool, someone who never had supported access can miss another opportunity. Employers can examine how they choose participants, provide learning time and recognize the work of testing and checking AI. More logins, by themselves, would not tell us whether those decisions had become fairer.
readerAnswers.action: If AI is being introduced where you work, a useful question is: “How can I join an approved trial, and what time and support are available to learn?” That asks for a concrete opportunity. It does not require you to buy a subscription, use AI outside your employer’s rules or turn your evenings into unpaid training.If you choose who gets training or project places, make the invitation and selection criteria visible. Include a supported route for people who have not already used the tool. Give participants time within their workload to try it, and include their experience when deciding whether and how to use it.Success should include useful work, sound judgment and recognition for the people contributing—not a target that everyone uses AI every day. Asking for access cannot guarantee that an employer provides it; responsibility for that decision remains with the employer.

explainBack: The figures measure representation and frequency separately. They do not identify ability or motives. Supported access and learning time are conditions an employer can examine, not a proven explanation for all of the gap.
unseenTransfer: If only existing users get invited to an AI trial, a manager should examine whether newcomers have a supported route in. Prior use alone does not tell us who is interested or able.
